title: The Most Common Speaking Mistakes Teachers Make: Part 1 hers-make-part-1/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Opening a three-part series on teacher speech, Linsin argues that how a teacher speaks profoundly affects listening, learning, and behavior—yet most teachers give it no thought. He identifies two initial mistakes: speaking too loudly, which paradoxically encourages students to tune out because it removes their responsibility to actively listen, and speaking over students who aren't yet fully quiet and attentive, which trains them to disregard instructions and provides them a ready excuse for not knowing what was said. His prescribed fixes are to consistently speak softly (reserving intensity for special dramatic effect) and to always wait until every student's eyes are on the teacher before beginning to speak, which he claims corrects both habits within about a week.
points: How a teacher speaks affects attentiveness, listening, independence, learning, and behavior—yet most teachers never examine their own speaking habits.
Speaking loudly counterintuitively causes students to tune out, since it removes their responsibility to actively listen closely.
Speaking calmly and softly compels students to lean in and pay closer attention, and preserves contrast for genuinely dramatic moments.
Talking over a class that isn't yet fully quiet gives students a built-in excuse for not knowing the directions and trains them to ignore the teacher's voice.
Fix: always wait until every student is silent and looking at the teacher before speaking, and keep the default voice calm and soft.
quotes: Little of classroom management, in fact, is untouched by the style, pace, inflection, pattern, and intensity of your speaking voice.
But speaking loudly causes students to tune out the sound of your voice, making it harder, not easier, for your message to get through.
Good teaching requires you to wait until all students are silent and looking at you before opening your mouth.
The reality is that when you speak loudly or talk over students who are unprepared to listen, you train them to disregard the sound of your voice.
The solution, though, is simple. Soften your voice and always confirm that every eye is on you before opening your mouth.
